834.title: Love, then do
834.hook: Augustine: love, and do what you will
834.howItsDone: Some Christians who draw on Augustine's teaching examine their motives at the end of the day, asking whether what they did and said came from love.

segments.voice: Yesterday, philos, the night before the cross. Your line was lay it down. What did you set down for a friend, and what did it cost? A new week starts today, with a bishop and five words. Day eight hundred thirty-four.

Love, and do what you will. On a poster, that sounds like permission. Follow your heart. Do your thing. But it comes from a sermon by Augustine, bishop of Hippo in North Africa, one of a series he preached on the same short letter we met this past week, First John. And in its setting it isn't permission at all. It's closer to a warning, and a harder rule than any list. Today: love, then do.
screen: `ON A POSTER, IT SOUNDS LIKE PERMISSION.` → `PREACHED BY A BISHOP.` → `A HARDER RULE THAN ANY LIST.`

segments.voice: First, the problem Augustine was looking at. The same outward act can come from opposite places. He gives examples. A father can be stern with his son, and a kidnapper can be gentle with a child he means to sell. Which one loves the boy? Not the gentle one. He reaches for the Gospel, too: the Father handed the Son over, and Judas handed him over. The same verb, says Augustine, but one acted from love and the other from betrayal. So you can't judge an act by how it looks from outside. Second, the sentence, offered as one short command. In Latin it runs, dilige, et quod vis fac: love, and do what you will. Third, what comes right after, which the poster leaves off. Augustine walks through it: if you keep quiet, keep quiet out of love. If you speak up, speak up out of love. If you correct someone, correct out of love. If you spare someone, spare them out of love. Let the root of love be inside, he says, and from that root nothing but good can grow. Fourth, why it's harder than a rule. A rule can be kept with a cold heart. You can follow every instruction and still be acting from spite, or pride, or fear. Augustine moves the test inside, to the root. Before the act, the question: is this coming from love? That's the order in today's line. Love first. Then do. Some readers hear a freedom in that; others hear a very high bar. It may be both.
screen: `THE SAME ACT, TWO ROOTS.` · `DILIGE, ET QUOD VIS FAC.` · `QUIET OR LOUD, FROM LOVE.` · `HARDER THAN A RULE.` · then, large: `LOVE, THEN DO.`

segments.voice: Let one thing you're about to do today come to mind: something you'll say, a message you'll send, a correction you need to make, a no you need to give. Breathe. Hold it up and look underneath it, the way Augustine asks. What's the root? Love for the person? Or the wish to win, to be right, to be left alone? You don't have to cancel the act. Just look. If the root isn't love yet, see whether the same act could come from love instead. If you pray, you can ask for that. The bell holds the time.
Love. In Augustine's sermon, the root every act should grow from: love, and then do what you will, whether you speak or stay silent. Today's word.
Your line: nothing but good can grow. Today, before the act you chose, pause for one breath and check its root. Day eight hundred thirty-four.

835.title: The little way
835.hook: Thérèse of Lisieux: small things done with great love
835.carry: nothing was too small to count
835.howItsDone: Catholics who follow Thérèse's little way offer small daily tasks and kindnesses to God, and some ask her prayers as Saint Thérèse, the Little Flower.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Augustine's five words. Your line was nothing but good can grow. When you checked the root of that one act, what did you find? Today, a young nun who took love down to the smallest size. Day eight hundred thirty-five.

In a Carmelite convent in Lisieux, in France, a young nun named Thérèse wanted to be a saint. But when she measured herself against the great saints, she writes, she felt like a grain of sand beside a mountain. She would never do anything that size. She was going to spend her life in a small enclosed house, doing laundry and chores, praying with the same few women every day. So she went looking for another road. Today: the little way.
screen: `A YOUNG NUN WANTS TO BE A SAINT.` → `A GRAIN OF SAND BESIDE A MOUNTAIN.` → `SHE LOOKS FOR ANOTHER ROAD.`

segments.voice: Thérèse tells this in her memoir, Story of a Soul, and the pictures she uses are homely. First, the elevator. She'd heard of elevators, an invention, she notes, that lifted people so they didn't have to climb. She was too small, she writes, to climb the rough staircase of perfection. She wanted an elevator. And she decided it was the arms of Jesus, lifting the little ones who can't climb. Second, flowers. Love, she says, proves itself by deeds, and she had no great deeds to give. So she would strew flowers: every small sacrifice, every glance, every kind word, offered with love. Nothing was too small to count. Third, the hardest one. There was a sister in the convent whose manner, Thérèse admits, she found deeply disagreeable. So she set out to treat that sister as she would the person she loved most. Whenever they met, she smiled, and she prayed for her. One day, she writes, the sister asked her what it was about her that Thérèse found so attractive. Fourth, the center. Underneath all of it is a discovery she writes about: in the heart of the Church, her vocation would be love. Not a role. A way of doing every small thing. Catholics honor her as a saint. Some readers find her way fits small lives: a nurse on night shift, a parent of toddlers, anyone whose day is mostly ordinary. The size of the act, in her way of seeing, isn't the measure. The love inside it is.
screen: `AN ELEVATOR, NOT A STAIRCASE.` · `STREWING FLOWERS.` · `THE SISTER SHE FOUND HARD.` · `HER VOCATION WOULD BE LOVE.` · then, large: `THE LITTLE WAY.`

segments.voice: Settle, and breathe. Run through the next few hours in your mind and pick the most ordinary thing waiting in them: a dish, an email, a diaper, a commute, a line at the store. Now picture doing that exact thing with great care, for someone, the way Thérèse strewed flowers. Not faster. Not bigger. Just with love inside it. Notice how small it is, and let that be fine. If you pray, you can offer it, the way she did. The bell holds the time.
Thérèse. The Carmelite nun who found her own road to sainthood in small deeds done with great love, like flowers strewn one at a time. Today's word.
Your line: nothing was too small to count. Today, do that one ordinary thing with love inside it, and tell no one. Day eight hundred thirty-five.

836.title: The Loving
836.hook: one of God's names in the Quran: the Loving
836.carry: love that is warm and shows
836.howItsDone: Muslims call on God by His names in prayer and remembrance, and some reflect on one name at a time, such as al-Wadud, the Loving, and try to show something of it in how they treat others.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Thérèse and her flowers. Your line was nothing was too small to count. Which ordinary thing did you do with love inside it? Today we turn to Muslim and Sufi voices, and a name. Day eight hundred thirty-six.

The Quran calls God by name after name. The Merciful. The Wise. The Hearing. The Seeing. In Muslim practice they are recited and reflected on, and some parents give them to their children, joined to the word Abd, servant: Abd al-Rahman, servant of the Merciful. One of the names is soft enough that it can catch a listener off guard. It isn't power, or knowledge, or judgment. It's warmth. Al-Wadud. The Loving. Today: where that name appears, and what sits right next to it.
screen: `GOD'S NAMES IN THE QURAN.` → `SERVANT OF THE MERCIFUL.` → `ONE NAME IS WARMTH.`

segments.voice: First, the word. Tradition links al-Wadud to wudd, an Arabic word for affection: not a distant goodwill, but love that is warm and shows. Elsewhere the Quran says that for those who believe and do good, the Merciful will appoint love, using that same word. Love, in this picture, is something God gives and also places between people. Second, the neighbors. The name appears in the chapter called al-Buruj, the Constellations, and Pickthall translates it like this: "And He is the Forgiving, the Loving." Forgiving and Loving, side by side. Some readers notice the order: forgiveness first, and then a love that is still there afterward, not a pardon given at arm's length. Third, the setting, which is the surprise. That chapter opens with a terrible story, the people of the ditch, a fire, and believers tormented only because they believed. A few verses later, the punishment it warns of is for those who persecute and "repent not." Some commentators point to those words: even for people that cruel, a door is described as still open. And right after comes the name: the Forgiving, the Loving. In another chapter the prophet Shuayb tells his people to ask pardon and turn back, and says, "Lo! my Lord is Merciful, Loving." Again, love beside mercy. Fourth, a Sufi voice. People tell a story about Rabia of Basra, an early woman mystic, carrying a torch and a bucket of water through the streets: to burn paradise and put out hell, she said, so that God would be loved for God alone. It's a story told, not a text. But it points at the same name.
screen: `WUDD: LOVE THAT SHOWS.` · `THE FORGIVING, THE LOVING.` · `A DOOR LEFT OPEN.` · `RABIA'S TORCH AND BUCKET.` · then, large: `AL-WADUD.`

segments.voice: Settle, and breathe. Ask yourself who could use a loving word today. Maybe someone you've had to forgive, or who has had to forgive you. Picture them. Now find one warm word, or a few, that you could actually say: I'm glad you called. Thank you for waiting for me. It's good to see you. Let it be simple and true. If you pray, you can call on God as al-Wadud, the Loving, in your own way. Then rest. The bell holds the time.
Al-Wadud. The Loving: one of God's names in the Quran, love that is warm and shows, set right beside the Forgiving. Today's word.
Your line: love that is warm and shows. Today, say that one warm word out loud to the person you pictured. Day eight hundred thirty-six.

screen: `DAY 836 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: WHAT YOU'D WANT FOR YOURSELF.`

837.title: What you'd want for yourself
837.hook: none of you truly believes until he loves for his brother what he loves for himself (Bukhari; Nawawi 13)
837.howItsDone: Muslims learn this hadith early, often from al-Nawawi's collection of forty hadith, and it is commonly memorized and quoted as a summary of how faith should show in the way a person treats others.

segments.voice: Yesterday, al-Wadud, one of God's names in the Quran: the Loving. Your line was love that is warm and shows. What loving word did you get to say? Today, the same love turned toward the person next to you. Day eight hundred thirty-seven.

Two slices of cake are left on the plate, and one is plainly bigger. Somebody has to cut, and somebody has to choose. Families have a trick for this: whoever cuts picks last. Suddenly the knife gets very careful. Nobody had to give a speech about fairness. The cutter simply has to treat the other slice as if it might be theirs. A short saying in the Islamic tradition asks for something like that, only it reaches past cake, all the way into faith itself. Today: wanting for someone else what you'd want for yourself.
screen: `TWO SLICES, ONE BIGGER.` → `THE CUTTER PICKS LAST.` → `AS IF IT WERE YOURS.`

segments.voice: First, the saying itself. It comes from the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, in the hadith collection of al-Bukhari, and the scholar al-Nawawi later placed it thirteenth in his little book of forty hadith. In plain words: none of you truly believes until he loves for his brother what he loves for himself. That's the whole saying. It's short enough to fit on a sticky note. Second, notice where it puts the test. It doesn't say none of you is polite, or none of you is generous. It says none of you truly believes. In this hadith, faith isn't finished in private. It shows up in what you wish for the person beside you. Third, notice the measuring stick. It isn't some ideal standard you have to look up. It's you. The saying trusts you to know what you'd want for yourself: to be forgiven quickly, to be given the benefit of the doubt, to have your name said kindly when you're not in the room. The saying takes that private wish list and turns it outward. Fourth, the word brother. Some readers hear it as a fellow Muslim. Others hear it widely, as any fellow human being. This lesson won't settle it for anyone. Either way, the motion is the same: the circle of what you want for yourself gets bigger by one. The Hebrew Bible has a neighbor in it too. Leviticus says, "thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself." Two scriptures, each saying it in its own words.
screen: `THE SAYING ITSELF.` · `WHERE IT PUTS THE TEST.` · `THE MEASURING STICK IS YOU.` · `THE WORD BROTHER.` · then, large: `WHAT YOU'D WANT FOR YOURSELF.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably and let your breath settle. Bring to mind one good thing you want for yourself right now. Maybe rest. Maybe a hard conversation going well. Maybe being understood. Hold it a moment and let it be clear. Now bring to mind one other person close by: someone at home, at work, or down the street. Picture that same good thing arriving for them. The same rest, the same understanding, no smaller slice. If it sticks, notice where. If you pray, you can hold that person in your own tradition's words. The bell holds the time.
Al-Bukhari. The hadith collection holding the Prophet's saying that none of you truly believes until he loves for his brother what he loves for himself. Today's word.
Your line: what I'd want. Once today, before you answer someone, ask what you'd want if you were on their side of the table, and give them that. Day eight hundred thirty-seven.

838.title: Mercy to the worlds
838.hook: the Prophet is called a mercy to the worlds (Quran 21:107)
838.howItsDone: Muslims begin recitation of the Quran's chapters, and many everyday tasks, with the Bismillah, which names God as merciful; the verse calling the Prophet a mercy to the worlds is often quoted when speaking of his character and example.

segments.voice: Yesterday, al-Bukhari's hadith about wanting for someone else what you'd want for yourself. Your line was what I'd want. Whose side of the table did you sit on? Today, one word with a very wide reach. Day eight hundred thirty-eight.

"In the name of Allah, the Beneficent, the Merciful." It is the first line of the Quran's opening chapter, and it stands at the head of chapter after chapter. It's written over doorways, said before meals, whispered before a long drive. Mercy is right there at the start, the frame around everything that follows. And in one short verse, the Quran turns that same word toward a person. Speaking to the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, it says he was sent as a mercy. Not to one town, or one people. To the worlds. Today: what it means to be called a mercy, and what that asks.
screen: `IN THE NAME OF ALLAH, THE MERCIFUL.` → `MERCY AT THE START.` → `SENT AS A MERCY.`

segments.voice: First, the verse. In the twenty-first surah, God addresses the Prophet and says, in plain words: we sent you only as a mercy to the worlds. It doesn't list his victories or his miracles. It names his purpose in one word. Second, the reach. The word translated worlds is the same one heard in the Quran's first chapter: "Praise be to Allah, Lord of the Worlds." So the mercy in this verse is as wide as the Lordship in that one. Some readers take it to include all people, and some widen it further, to animals and the whole of creation. Third, mercy in small things. The hadith collections keep stories of the Prophet's gentleness: being patient with children who climbed on him during prayer, telling of a person forgiven for giving water to a thirsty dog. One saying puts it simply: those who show mercy are shown mercy by the Most Merciful. In these stories, mercy is not a mood. It's something done, often for someone who can't repay it. Fourth, mercy as a pattern. Elsewhere the Quran tells believers that in the Prophet "ye have a good example," and so this verse is also an invitation. If he was sent as a mercy, those who love him try, in their own small way, to be one. Mercy here means meeting someone who has no claim on you, and treating them better than they've earned.
screen: `THE VERSE: SENT AS A MERCY.` · `AS WIDE AS THE WORLDS.` · `MERCY IN SMALL THINGS.` · `MERCY AS A PATTERN.` · then, large: `MERCY TO THE WORLDS.`

segments.voice: Sit and let your shoulders drop. Think back over the last few days for one moment where someone was at your mercy, even slightly. A slow cashier. A child who spilled something. A coworker who missed a deadline that landed on you. Bring that moment back as clearly as you can. Now replay it with mercy in it: a softer word, a little more time, no sigh. You don't have to fix the past. Just let your body rehearse the gentler version. If you pray, you can ask for mercy in your own tradition's words. The bell holds the time.
Raḥmatan. The Quran's word for the Prophet's purpose: sent as a mercy reaching every world, not just one town or people. Today's word.
Your line: mercy. Once today, when someone is at your mercy, even for a moment, give them a little more patience than they've earned. Day eight hundred thirty-eight.

839.title: Layla and Majnun
839.hook: Nizami's tale: Qays loves Layla to madness, and Sufis read it as longing for God
839.howItsDone: The story of Layla and Majnun is told and sung across the Muslim world, and Sufi poets and teachers use Majnun as an image of the lover of God who gives up everything for the Beloved.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Quran's raḥmatan, mercy to the worlds. Your line was mercy. Who got a little more patience from you than they'd earned? Today, a love story that doesn't end the way love stories are supposed to. Day eight hundred thirty-nine.

A boy named Qays sits in a schoolroom and can't stop looking at a girl named Layla. She looks back. By the time the grown-ups notice, it's too late: he's composing poems about her, out loud, in the street. People start calling him by a new name, Majnun, the one who has lost his mind. The story was told in Arabic poetry and retold by the Persian poet Nizami, and poets kept retelling it after him. Today: a madman of love, and why Sufis kept telling his story.
screen: `QAYS SEES LAYLA.` → `POEMS IN THE STREET.` → `THEY CALL HIM MAJNUN.`

segments.voice: First, the story. In Nizami's telling, Layla's family keep her away from Qays, and her father refuses the marriage. She is married to another man. Qays leaves the town and goes into the wilderness, where he lives among wild animals and sings his poems to her across the sand. The two never really live together. In the end, both die still apart. Second, why it isn't only a tragedy. Sufis, the mystics of Islam, read Majnun as a picture of the soul. The lover who gives up reputation, comfort and good sense for one beloved looks, to them, like the seeker who gives up everything for God. Layla becomes a sign of the divine beauty the soul is looking for. Third, a moment from Rumi. In his Masnavi, Rumi tells of a caliph who asks to see the famous Layla. He looks her over and shrugs: you're no more beautiful than other women. And Layla answers, in effect: be quiet, you are not Majnun. Beauty here lives in the eyes of the lover. To someone outside, the beloved seems ordinary. Fourth, what madness means here. Majnun's madness isn't confusion. It's a love so complete that ordinary sense can't contain it. Sufi poets return to that image: to love God fully may look foolish from outside. The story keeps both readings. A boy and a girl who loved and lost. And a soul that won't stop looking for what it loves.
screen: `A LOVE KEPT APART.` · `THE SOUL AS MAJNUN.` · `YOU ARE NOT MAJNUN.` · `WHAT MADNESS MEANS HERE.` · then, large: `LAYLA AND MAJNUN.`

segments.voice: If you have one nearby, find an old love letter, a card, or a message from someone who loved you, or whom you loved. If not, bring one back from memory. Read it slowly, or remember it slowly. Don't judge how it ended. Notice only how the words looked at the other person: what they saw that nobody else saw. Let your breath stay easy while you read. Then set it down and sit with whatever it stirred. If you pray, you can bring that longing into your own tradition's words. The bell holds the time.
Majnun. The name given to Qays for his love of Layla, read by Sufis as the soul's own longing for God. Today's word.
Your line: mad with love. Once today, look at someone you love the way Majnun looked at Layla, and notice one thing in them a stranger would miss. Day eight hundred thirty-nine.

840.title: The astrolabe
840.hook: Rumi: love is the astrolabe of God's mysteries (Masnavi 1.110)
840.carry: a love you can look through
840.howItsDone: The Masnavi is read and recited in Sufi circles, often line by line with commentary, and its opening story of the king and the servant girl is where readers meet this line about love as an astrolabe.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Layla and Majnun, the boy called mad for love. Your line was mad with love. What did you see in someone that a stranger would miss? Today, Rumi picks up an instrument. Day eight hundred forty.

How do you read the night sky with something that fits in your hands? In the medieval Islamic world, one answer was a brass disk covered in fine lines and tiny engraved names. A pointer swings across the front. A ring hangs from the top so it can dangle straight down from your thumb. It's an astrolabe. Held up to the night sky and sighted on a star, it could help its owner tell the hour, or work out where in the heavens things stood. In Rumi's world, it was the kind of tool a learned person carried to read the sky. And in one line of his Masnavi, Rumi says love is exactly that kind of instrument. Today: love as the astrolabe.
screen: `A BRASS DISK OF FINE LINES.` → `SIGHTED ON A STAR.` → `LOVE IS AN INSTRUMENT.`

segments.voice: First, where the line sits. Near the start of the Masnavi, after its opening song of the reed, comes the story of a king who falls in love with a servant girl, and she falls ill. Doctors can't cure her. A wise physician finally sees the truth: her sickness is love. Right there, Rumi steps out of the story and says, in plain words, that the lover's ailment is unlike every other ailment, and love is the astrolabe of God's mysteries. Second, what the astrolabe does. You don't look at an astrolabe for its own sake. You look through it, at the sky. So Rumi isn't saying love is the mystery. He's saying love is how you take a reading of it. Third, the next line. Rumi goes on, again in paraphrase: whether love is of this world or of the other, in the end it leads us there. A love for a person, a place, a piece of music: in his view, any of these, sighted carefully, points beyond itself. Fourth, this week. We heard love called a command to act, and a little way of small things. We met al-Wadud, the Loving. We wished for someone else what we'd want for ourselves, and heard of a mercy as wide as the worlds. Yesterday Majnun went mad with love. Today Rumi hands us the instrument for all of it: a love you can look through, toward its source.
screen: `A SICKNESS THAT IS LOVE.` · `YOU LOOK THROUGH IT.` · `IT LEADS US THERE.` · `A WEEK OF LOVE.` · then, large: `THE ASTROLABE.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably and choose one thing you love. A person, a song, a stretch of coastline, a dog. Hold it in mind clearly. Now, like sighting along an astrolabe, look through it instead of at it. Ask quietly: what is it in this that I love? Then ask again of the answer. Kindness? Where does kindness come from? Beauty? What is it pointing toward? Follow it back step by step, as far as it goes, without forcing an answer at the end. If you pray, you can let the trail lead into your own tradition's words. The bell holds the time.
The astrolabe. Rumi's picture of love in the Masnavi: an instrument you look through to read God's mysteries, not the mystery itself. Today's word.
Your line: a love you can look through. Once today, when something you love catches you, look through it for a moment and ask what it's pointing toward. Day eight hundred forty.
